books.section: Topic 6.7 Labor in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Samuel Gompers, address to the International Labor Congress (August 28, 1893)

options.misconception: This pair is about work and crime, not about schooling.
options.text: More constant work and less crime.

options.misconception: This pair is about free time, not about schooling.
This pair is about courts and fairness, not about schooling.

rationales.A: Constant work and less crime say nothing about schools or learning.
rationales.B: Leisure and greed say nothing about schools or learning.
rationales.C: Schoolhouses are schools, and Gompers pairs them with books and learning later in the list.
rationales.D: Justice and revenge are about fairness in the courts, not about schooling.
rationales.general:
Match each pair to the idea in the stem.
1. The stem asks for education.
2. Constant work is about jobs, leisure is about free time, and justice is about the courts.
3. Only schoolhouses name a place of learning.
4. Gompers also asks for more books and more learning, which point the same way.
Remember: match the key word in the stem to the key word in the choice.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: Which pair from the passage best shows Gompers linking labor’s demands to education?

stimulus.source_note: Samuel Gompers, address to the International Labor Congress, August 28, 1893. Public domain (Samuel Gompers Papers, University of Maryland).
stimulus.text: “What does labor want? . . . We want more schoolhouses and less jails; more books and less arsenals; more learning and less vice; more constant work and less crime; more leisure and less greed; more justice and less revenge; in fact, more of the opportunities to cultivate our better natures, to make manhood more noble, womanhood more beautiful and childhood more happy and bright.”
